images.title: Arcs that fall short
images.purpose: Show that on an 8 cm base, arcs of 3 cm and 4 cm do not meet, leaving a gap.
images.composition: A long horizontal base across the middle; two short arcs at the ends with a visible gap between them.
exact_structure: A horizontal teal (#0072B2) segment AB labelled 8 cm, with dots at A (left end) and B (right end).
A short amber (#E69F00) arc centred at A of radius 3 cm, bulging up and right, ending on AB at a point 3 cm from A, with a thin bracket labelled 3 cm under AB.
A short reddish purple (#CC79A7) arc centred at B of radius 4 cm, bulging up and left, ending on AB at a point 4 cm from B, with a thin bracket labelled 4 cm under AB.
Between the end of the amber reach and the start of the purple reach there is a clear gap (1 cm, since 8 is more than 3 + 4 = 7), shown as a vermilion (#D55E00) double headed arrow labelled gap.
The two arcs do not touch or cross anywhere.
rejection: no visible gap between the arcs
brackets that reach the whole base
any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: When the two short lengths together are less than the long one, the arcs cannot meet.
images.description: An 8 cm base with a 3 cm arc from A and a 4 cm arc from B that leave a gap.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video for this concept.
images.teaching_notes: Add 3 and 4, compare with 8 and point at the gap.

image_decisions.why: Seeing the arcs fall short is the core of why some lengths fail.
